title: The register
hook: Umar sets up stipends, including for the poor and newborns (reported)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the calendar, moon months and a year one. Your line was counted from the migration.

A baby is crying behind a door in Medina, and it will not stop. Not the ordinary crying of a tired baby; this one goes on and on. A man walking the streets in the dark stops at the door and tells the mother to look after her child. Later he passes again, and the baby is still crying. He asks what's wrong. She doesn't know who she's speaking to. She is weaning the child early, she tells him, because the stipend is only paid for children once they are weaned. The man walking the streets is Umar. Today's word: the register behind that rule.
screen: `A BABY CRYING IN THE NIGHT.` → `WEANED EARLY, FOR THE STIPEND.` → `THE MAN AT THE DOOR IS UMAR.`

segments.voice: Diwan means a register: a book of names. The histories say Umar set one up in Medina as wealth began to come in, listing the people of the community so that each could receive a regular share, an ata, from the public treasury. The reports describe the Prophet's family, the companions, the fighters and their households, written in by name. It sounds dry: a list. But a list decides who counts. Now back to the crying baby. This part comes from the early histories, not the hadith collections, and is told as a story. When the mother explains, Umar is shaken. Tradition says that at the dawn prayer the people could hardly understand his recitation for his weeping, and that afterward he said something like: woe to Umar, how many children has he harmed? Then he had it announced: do not hurry to wean your children; we will give a share for every child born in Islam. From birth, not from weaning. The Qur'an says mothers may nurse their children for two whole years, for those who want to complete the nursing. A rule written for the treasury had quietly pushed against that, and against a baby's hunger. And look at what Umar did not say. He didn't blame the mother. He didn't defend the rule because it was his. He looked at who the rule was hurting, and he rewrote it. A register is only as just as the people it remembers to write in.
screen: `DIWAN: A REGISTER OF NAMES.` · `A REGULAR SHARE FROM THE TREASURY.` · `A RULE THAT HURT A BABY.` · `FROM BIRTH, NOT FROM WEANING.` · then, large: `A SHARE FOR EVERY CHILD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone raising a little one with very little help, a new baby or one on the way, and picture their night: the crying, the tiredness, the counting of money. If you pray, ask for ease for them; if not, simply hold them in mind with care for a moment.
Diwan. A register of names: in Umar's time, the list that gave each person in the community a regular share from the treasury, and, the story says, every child from birth. Today's word.
Your line: a share for every child. From birth, not from weaning. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims often retell the story of Umar and the crying baby in sermons on justice and care for the vulnerable, and the diwan is taught in Islamic history as an early public register.

fork.setup: you're Umar. you learn a mother is weaning her baby early because your rule only pays for weaned children. what do you do?
options: keep the rule; rules are rules.
give that one mother some money quietly.
change the rule so every child has a share from birth.
fork.reveal: the story says he had it announced: don't hurry to wean your children; a share for every child born in Islam.

original.note: Arabic: a register or record of names; under Umar, the list of those owed a share from the treasury.

chat.says: Why did Umar change the rule about the children's stipend?
options: In the story, a mother weaned early for the stipend, so he paid from birth.
Too many families complained that the treasury paid them too slowly.
The Qur'an forbids weaning, so the rule had to be changed to match.
chat.meaning: The story says a crying baby, weaned early for the stipend, shook Umar; he announced a share for every child from birth.
